title: Yes These Are Concerning
author: Ben Riley
summary: Ben Riley responds to an online campaign against him following his investigative report on Alpha School's student boot camp, turning a rebuttal of personal smears into a sharper critique of the AI-driven school's practices. He argues that supporters insinuating he is dangerous for inviting student DMs have, in effect, made his case: if adults contacting minors on Twitter is a risk, then Alpha School's policy requiring students to hold verified accounts, gain 100 followers, and tweet daily is the real problem. Riley frames the backlash as cognitive dissonance within a school culture built on relentless affirmation of its own superiority, and he points to an Alpha staff member as an example. He then reveals that Carl Hendrick, a prominent Alpha advisor and longtime colleague in the cognitive-science-in-education movement, privately called his findings 'concerning' before publicly continuing to defend the school. The essay closes by noting mainstream interest from major outlets and a Fordham Institute post comparing Alpha to Theranos, and by recommitting to the investigation as a matter of duty. Because the piece's subject is the practices and credibility of an AI-first school model, it is filed in Ed-Tech.
points: Riley turns critics' insinuations against Alpha School, arguing that a school requiring minors to maintain public Twitter accounts with follower targets is itself exposing students to online predators.
He recommends Johann Neem's Democracy's Schools to argue that public education and democracy are intertwined and are eroding together.
Alpha's rule barring adult guides from talking with children to avoid 'compromising its model' is contrasted with the normal human expectation that adults and kids converse.
Carl Hendrick privately told Riley the boot camp findings were concerning, yet publicly doubled down on defending Alpha, which Riley treats as a telling contradiction.
Riley reports that Alpha has confirmed the boot camp's biometric monitoring and week-long discovery learning requirement, and that outlets including the New York Times and NPR have sought comment.
quotes: Many appear to have no official relationship with Alpha, but they are no doubt attracted to its public posturing as “the future of AI-driven education” or whatever, and maybe more importantly, its repeated denigration of so-called normal school.

It’s a lovely history that tells a comprehensive story that too few Americans appreciate, namely, that democracy and public education, emphasis on public, are bound together. It is no coincidence they are eroding in tandem too.
The world is filled with people both good and evil, and social media attracts the latter because of its cloak of anonymity, so forcing children to use it is wrong. Stop doing it, Alpha School!
They require students to obtain verified Twitter accounts and gain 100 followers and tweet every day. This was Alpha School leadership’s decision. They own it.

What’s happening right now within Alpha School is massive cognitive dissonance, and Wendy is Exhibit A. Alpha School has deliberately cultivated a culture that depends on triumphal and relentless affirmation of its superiority.

Alpha School may prohibit its adult “guides” from talking to children so as to not “compromise its model,” but out here in the Land of the Normal, adults and kids can have conversations. It’s fundamental to being human, actually.
Yet, sadly but also infuriatingly, to my knowledge Carl’s never expressed publicly what he said to me privately. Instead, he has since doubled down on his defense of Alpha School on social media.

My arguments won’t persuade them, in fact they won’t even make sense to them, because we live in separate cognitive worlds, with values that are an anethma to each other. There is no cognitive resonance between us.
